title: Security
intro: agent.dfx.swiss encrypts your content in this browser before it leaves your device. This page shows which build the server delivered and what the server can and cannot see.
unavailable: Not available – the build manifest could not be loaded.
build.title: Delivered build
build.mismatch: Warning: the build manifest names a different platform root key than the code running in this browser. Do not sign in and contact support.
build.compare: The build hash is the SHA-256 of build-manifest.json as the server delivers it, computed here by the delivered code itself – so this page can confirm a build, but cannot prove it against a dishonest server. To check independently, download build-manifest.json from this address with a separate tool (for example curl and sha256sum) and compare its hash with the one published for this version. Anyone can reproduce a release: check out the commit and run npm ci and npm run build with VITE_PLATFORM_ROOT_KEY set to the published platform root key; the files and the build hash are byte-identical.
sees.title: What the server sees
sees.body: To route data, enforce rights and show status, the hub stores the following in plaintext:
sees.ids: IDs of organizations, workgroups, tasks, sessions, operations, devices, users, events and whiteboard entries
sees.logs: membership and platform logs: roles, access rights, public keys, invitation IDs, device assignments, key epochs
sees.passkeys: passkey credential IDs and public keys, sign counters and session public keys
sees.headers: event headers (kind, scope, key epoch, author, task, session, referenced event, log position, time), sizes and receive times
sees.states: task and session states and times, the device, the VM, the parent session and depth, the model access kind and model ID
sees.operations: operation type, state, decision, error code, duplicate tag and timestamps
sees.metrics: resource metrics, token counters, cost, context-window share and subscription quota percentages
sees.notifications: notification records (recipient, kind, target IDs) and your settings (model preference, language)
sees.audit: audit and read-log rows (who did what to which ID, with the result; for a session's read also the workgroup it read and the person whose instruction it followed) and credential metadata (owner, kind, version)
hidden.title: What the server cannot see
hidden.body: Everything else stays encrypted end to end; the server never has the keys to open it:
hidden.content: prompts, answers, tool calls, file changes, terminal output and whiteboard entries
hidden.names: names of organizations, workgroups, tasks, members and devices
hidden.keys: the outputs of your passkeys, your private keys and the keys of organizations and workgroups
hidden.credentials: the values of your credentials (API keys, subscription tokens, GitHub access)
javascript.title: Trust in the delivered code
javascript.body: Encryption in a web browser depends on the JavaScript the server delivers. A strict content security policy, integrity hashes on the scripts of the start page and a reproducible build limit this risk, but a compromised server could still deliver changed code, also for parts that load later (terminal, charts, formatted text). This page cannot detect that by itself; only an independent comparison of the build hash with the published one can.
devices.title: Execution devices
devices.body: The devices that run your tasks decrypt the content of the workgroups assigned to them: they process prompts, files and answers in plaintext. Assign only devices you trust; removing a device from a workgroup rotates the workgroup's keys. A session may also read other workgroups of these devices that both the task owner and the person instructing it may read; what it writes from them into its own workgroup becomes readable for everybody who reads that workgroup.
community.title: Community
community.body: Community messages are readable by every user of the platform; they are not confidential like tasks, whiteboards and credentials. Encryption keeps their text and the sender names out of the server's database and backups, but a manipulated server could read messages and even write messages in another user's name. Do not share anything confidential there.
